class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>La gente se relaja en las icónicas sillas verdes del Jardín de Luxemburgo de París. El Distrito de Parques de Chicago dijo que sillas similares “traerán un pedazo de Francia al jardín delantero de Chicago”.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jacques Brinon/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Si bien la fuente es indudablemente uno de los monumentos más icónicos de la ciudad, la falta de asientos cercanos ha sido tema de conversación local durante años. En 2022, el residente de Chicago, Rick Weber, inició una conversación en Twitter (ahora X) al publicar lo que observó un día cerca de la fuente: visitantes tomándose fotos y luego marchándose, ya que no había dónde sentarse y los puestos de comida cercanos estaban cerrados.</p><p>En el programa de talk show de WBEZ, Reset, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/reset-with-sasha-ann-simons/2022/05/24/why-arent-chicagos-public-spaces-more-like-europes" target="_blank" >Weber y otros invitados hablaron</a> sobre cómo Chicago debería alinearse más con los parques públicos de ciudades como París. “Esto se supone que es el porche delantero de Chicago, ¿verdad?” dijo Weber en ese momento. “Entonces, ¿qué tipo de hospitalidad extendemos no solo a nuestros propios ciudadanos, sino a las personas que nos visitan aquí?”.</p><p>Ahora, la Municipalidad ha lanzado un plan que lleva años en desarrollo. Las 100 sillas que debutaron este fin de semana son parte de una iniciativa más grande, llamada “<a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagoparkdistrict.com/featured-capital-projects#132756" target="_blank" >El Jardín Frontal de Chicago Reimaginado 2026</a>,” que fue publicada en febrero como una actualización a un plan de 2002. Una de las ideas más ambiciosas del nuevo plan movería el DuSable Lake Shore Drive bajo tierra por un tramo y ampliaría el paisajismo que rodea la Fuente de Buckingham hasta el frente del lago.</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers es reportera de artes y cultura en WBEZ. </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: What you need to know about Illinois' new cellphone ban in schools
entries.summary: <p>Illinois is set to join a growing number of states that have barred cellphone use in the classroom.</p><p>Just as the Illinois General Assembly reached its deadline to wrap up its legislative session Sunday, the state Senate passed <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2026/04/28/illinois-bill-to-ban-school-cell-phone-use-moves-forward/" target="_blank" >legislation that would largely restrict cellphones</a><b> </b>in Illinois schools. The <a class="Link" href="https://ilga.gov/Legislation/BillStatus?DocNum=2427&GAID=18&DocTypeID=SB&LegID=162470&SessionID=114&SpecSess=&Session=&GA=104#actions" target="_blank" >legislation would go into effect for the 2027-28 school year</a>, meaning school districts will have a year to plan before the restrictions are implemented.</p><p>The bill now heads to <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2025/02/19/illinois-pritzker-propose-to-ban-cellphones/" target="_blank" >Gov. JB Pritzker, who has been a vocal advocate for limiting cellphone use</a> in the classroom. It’s quite the turnaround in the Illinois state legislature, which <a class="Link" href="https://www.chalkbeat.org/chicago/2025/06/25/illinois-lawmakers-failed-to-pass-school-cellphone-restriction-bill/" target="_blank" >failed to pass the bill in the state House of Representatives despite unanimous Senate approval</a><b> </b>during last year’s session.</p><p>Cellphones aren’t the only devices the bill bars from the classroom — tablets, laptops, gaming consoles, and smart watches are also banned. School-issued devices are exempt from the ban.</p><p>These broad restrictions aim to improve students’ academic performance by removing the distraction of what the bill calls “wireless communication devices,” proponents say. Barring them from classrooms could also “strengthen friendships and human interactions, and minimize bullying,” said Jessica Handy, executive director of Stand for Children Illinois.</p><p>The cellphone ban wasn’t the only legislation taking aim at children’s device usage that lawmakers passed this week. Another bill heading to Pritzker’s desk outlines limitations on social media platforms’ algorithms to protect children’s privacy. Both bills received bipartisan support from state lawmakers — something Pritzker said underscored the urgency of addressing the effects of cellphones on children.</p><p>“We’re giving children more classroom focus and a better education by banning kids’ use of cellphones during the school day from start to finish,” Pritzker said at a Monday news conference.</p><p>Research on the effectiveness of banning cellphones in schools is still preliminary, but results have been largely mixed. An <a class="Link" href="https://tom-dee.github.io/files/w35132.pdf" target="_blank" >April study published by the National Bureau of Economic Research showed a reduction in phone usage</a> in schools with storage pouches for phones, but also found a minimal impact on student test scores or attendance.</p><p>Thirty-five other states have <a class="Link" href="https://ballotpedia.org/State_policies_on_cellphone_use_in_K-12_public_schools" target="_blank" >enacted legislation that bans or limits cellphone use in the classroom</a> over the past few years, according to Ballotpedia.</p><p>Some changes from last year’s version of the bill include exceptions to ensure student safety, and limits on punitive measures against children who violate the bans. For example, after members of the legislative Black Caucus and Stand for Children expressed concern that students of color could be disproportionately disciplined, lawmakers added a section disallowing suspensions, expulsions, and fines against students who violate their district’s policy.</p><p>Several other exceptions are also folded into the legislation. Devices can be exempted from the policy if:<br></p><ul id="rte-204adec1-5ec2-11f1-9a1a-b3b6c1ce6872"><li>A healthcare professional has determined it is medically necessary.</li><li>It is used for an Individualized Education Program, which outlines accommodations for students with disabilities.</li><li>The student is a caregiver responsible for a family member.</li><li>An English language learner uses it for translation.</li><li>A school staff member has allowed the use of the device.</li><li>An emergency occurs.</li><li>A school district allows usage during high school lunch breaks and periods between classes.</li><li>Over the next year, school districts must figure out how to store students’ restricted devices, because the bill doesn’t specify how schools must do so. If a device “stored in good faith” is damaged, school staff cannot be held liable, according to the bill. Some organizations such as the Illinois Federation of Teachers previously seemed hesitant about storage guidance, specifically what it might cost schools to implement.</li></ul><p>The State Board of Education will provide a template for school cellphone policies by September. Feedback from local teachers unions is required, and student input is encouraged to help districts develop their policies.</p><p>Once the policies go into effect, parents can find their school’s rules on their district website or student handbook.<br></p>

entries.title: Man and woman found dead in Bellwood home
entries.summary: <p>An emergency response to a west suburban Bellwood home led to the discovery of two dead adults early Monday, officials said. </p><p>A unidentified woman and man were pronounced dead at 2:10 a.m. and at 2:28 p.m., respectively, inside a small brick house in the 1000 block of 32nd Avenue, police and the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>They two were taken to Loyola University Medical Center in Maywood, Bellwood fire officials said. </p><p>Details on the circumstances of the incident were not immediately available. </p>

entries.title: Bengals will hold joint practice vs. Bears in August
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a>’ remodeled defense will be tested by Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow two days before the two teams play in a preseason game this August.</p><p>The Bengals will host the Bears for a joint practice Aug. 20, Bengals coach Zac Taylor told Cincinnati reporters on Tuesday. The two teams will then face off at Paycor Stadium on Aug. 22.</p><p>The matchup will pit brother against brother, with the Bengals head coach facing off against Press Taylor, the Bears’ first-year offensive coordinator. Press Taylor was Ben Johnson’s pass-game coordinator last season when the Bears beat the Burrow-less Bengals.</p><p>“That’s my brother, but he’s also a football coach,” Press Taylor said last month. “We share the same interest. Football tends to come up when we’re talking. Things like that come up quite a bit.”</p><p>The Bears have practiced against Burrow before. In 2024, the Bears <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/08/14/bears-training-camo-bengals-vow-best-behavior-nfl-crack-down-practice-fights" target="_blank" >hosted the Bengals</a> for a joint practice at Halas Hall. The rainy practice, during which the Bengals suffered two serious injuries, was featured on the third episode of “Hard Knocks.”</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module entries.title: El olor que emite una planta en el lado sureste no tiene la prioridad que le darían en el lado norte
entries.summary: <p>Los veranos en Chicago son sagrados. Después de meses de frío brutal, la ciudad cobra vida. En mi vecindario, los veranos son diferentes.</p><p>Durante años, hemos estado atrapados en nuestras propias casas debido a los olores provenientes de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2025/07/09/pullman-innovations-odor-pollution-violations-chicago-health-epa-peter-chico" target="_blank" >Pullman Innovations</a>, una instalación de refinación de aceites y grasas ubicada en el 2701 E. 100th St. El hedor permea nuestra ropa, nuestros autos, los abrigos de nuestros hijos.</p><p>Se filtra a través de las ventanas cerradas y mantiene a los vecinos despiertos por la noche. Los residentes que viven a varias cuadras de distancia usan mascarillas en sus casas y queman incienso solo para soportar la noche.</p><p>Los inspectores de la Municipalidad han descrito el olor en sus informes como "<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz/2025/07/11/vecinos-enfurecen-por-el-olor-a-podrido-de-fabrica-del-lado-sur" target="_blank" >pescado en descomposición/descomposición de carne</a>". Uno <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2023/2/10/23592110/polluters-pullman-innovations-air-quality-pollution-violations" target="_blank" >escribió</a> que "me provocó náuseas al instante y quise vomitar". Los inspectores pudieron irse. Mis vecinos no.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-6e0000" name="module-6e0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Si esto sucediera en Lincoln Park por un solo día, la instalación sería cerrada con un candado antes del atardecer. Pero la planta no está en Lincoln Park. Está en el lado sureste, en la comunidad trabajadora afroamericana y latina donde crecí y donde estoy criando a mis hijos.</p><p>En lugar de acción, recibimos declaraciones. Citaciones menores. Promesas sobre nuevos controles de olor que la empresa ha estado haciendo desde 2016, cuando asumió el control de un propietario anterior que acumuló cientos de quejas antes de quebrar al enfrentar una demanda estatal.</p><p>Esto no es sólo una inconveniencia. Son fiestas de cumpleaños canceladas. Los abuelos no pueden sentarse en sus porches y los padres han llevado a sus hijos del parque porque se vomitan. Los químicos utilizados ahí causan náuseas, dolores de cabeza y problemas respiratorios.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Una vista aérea muestra Pullman Innovations, empresa ubicada en el 2701 E. 100th St., en el extremo sureste de la ciudad, que fabrica y distribuye aceite vegetal, en 2023.</p></figcaption></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>La situación está empeorando. El año pasado, la Agencia de Protección Ambiental de Illinois (EPA) dijo que Pullman Innovations falló en "obtener a tiempo un permiso de construcción previo a la construcción" para una enorme caldera industrial. La empresa está expandiendo silenciosamente una instalación que ya no puede controlar lo que emite junto a un parque público.</p><p>Estamos de acuerdo con los funcionarios estatales que han criticado la reducción de las protecciones ambientales a nivel federal. Ahora demuéstrenme que lo dicen en serio. Detengan cualquier construcción sin permiso. Revoquen los permisos de operación. Cierren esta instalación. Dejen de permitir que una refinería de aceite para alimentos para aves le haga la vida imposible a los residentes de Chicago porque vivimos al sur de 95th Street.</p><p>No estamos pidiendo otra reunión. Estamos pidiendo la misma protección que recibiría cualquier vecindario del lado norte en cualquier día de la semana.</p><p><i>Gina Ramírez, residente del lado sureste y directora de Salud Ambiental del Medio Oeste, Consejo de Defensa de Recursos Nacionales </i></p><h3>Ira al volante</h3><p>Cada parte del cerebro tiene funciones específicas. El lóbulo frontal se encarga de pensar, planificar, tomar decisiones y mantener la atención.</p><p>¿Acaso la pandemia de COVID-19 borró esa función de nosotros?.</p><p>Tomé mi última prueba de manejo a los 80 años y el examinador dijo que era un conductor excelente. Recordando cuando obtuve mi licencia en la escuela secundaria en 1960, casi reprobé el examen porque "me pasé" una señal de alto mientras giraba a la derecha.</p><p>Avancemos hasta 2026. ¿Por qué tenemos límites de velocidad publicados?, nadie los respeta. Las calles están llenas de automovilistas que exceden el límite de velocidad, y hay numerosos atropellos con víctimas mortales.</p><p>¿Qué pasa con las autopistas? El límite de velocidad publicado es de 55 millas por hora en las áreas urbanas de Illinois. Sin embargo, si voy a 60 o 65 millas por hora (sí, por encima del límite), me rebasan otros que van a 70 y 80 millas por hora. Cada día hay informes de accidentes que involucran dos, tres o cuatro autos, o un camión volcado con heridos y muertes.</p><p>Algunas infracciones de las "Reglas de la carretera" que a menudo veo: exceso de velocidad, no ceder el paso a un peatón, cambios de carril excesivos, girar a la izquierda donde hay una señal de "solo vuelta a la derecha" y bloquear un acceso o intersección donde dice "No bloquear".</p><p>¿Son ciegos estos conductores? No. Si lo fueran, no podrían conducir, así que le atribuyo esto a la estupidez y la imprudencia.</p><p>El personal de tráfico de la Municipalidad y del estado necesita ser más activo en nuestras carreteras para frenar todas estas infracciones. Debe haber consecuencias por este comportamiento al volante.</p><p>¡Esta epidemia necesita atención inmediata!</p><p><i>Dick Nelson, West Ridge </i></p><h3>La política de inteligencia artificial debe ser equilibrada y beneficiosa para todos</h3><p>Los legisladores de Illinois tienen razón al tomarse en serio la inteligencia artificial (AI). A principios de este mes, el Senado estatal avanzó con un nuevo <a class="Link" href="https://capitolnewsillinois.com/news/bill-regulating-powerful-ai-models-advances-as-advocates-say-its-only-the-first-step/" target="_blank" >marco de política de AI</a> destinado a proteger a los consumidores, mejorar la transparencia y abordar los riesgos reales que surgen a medida que la AI se convierte en parte de la vida cotidiana.</p><p>Como alguien que trabaja en la comunidad de nuevas empresas “startups” de Chicago, me alegra que nuestros legisladores estén priorizando la política de AI. La AI plantea preguntas serias, especialmente en torno a la seguridad en línea, la infancia, la salud mental, la discriminación y la protección del consumidor.</p><p>Y en ausencia de un marco nacional, los estados no pueden simplemente esperar a ver qué hará Washington, D.C.</p><p>Mientras tanto, los legisladores en Springfield deben reconocer la delgada línea que están cruzando. Illinois necesita una política de AI que proteja a las personas sin hacer imposible que las nuevas empresas se desarrollen aquí.</p><p>Ese equilibrio es especialmente importante en áreas como los chatbots y la responsabilidad. Las reglas que rigen cómo las herramientas de AI interactúan con los usuarios, qué divulgaciones son necesarias y cuándo las empresas pueden ser consideradas responsables son clave.</p><p>Pero no podemos regular a las grandes empresas tecnológicas de la misma manera que a las startups. Para las primeras, navegar por las distintas reglas de cada estado es una molestia. Para las últimas, una política bien intencionada pero excesiva podría causar que se cierren las puertas por completo.</p><p>Por eso, Illinois debe tener cuidado de no crear una estructura regulatoria aislada que se sume a un mosaico creciente de leyes estatales. Un camino mucho mejor sería trabajar en conjunto con otros estados líderes, incluidos California y Nueva York, para crear mayor predictibilidad para los creadores, al tiempo que se preservan sólidas protecciones para los consumidores.</p><p>California ha establecido un importante precedente al centrar sus requisitos de cumplimiento más significativos en los desarrolladores de AI más grandes y poderosos. Nueva York ha seguido un camino similar utilizando el marco de California en lugar de empezar desde cero. Este enfoque reconoce el valor de alinear las políticas con los principales centros tecnológicos de nuestra nación. También reconoce que las grandes empresas tecnológicas y las startups no son lo mismo, y no deberían ser reguladas como si lo fueran.</p><p>Illinois puede acertar con la política de AI. Pero si no lo hacemos, corremos el riesgo de convertirnos en un lugar donde solo las empresas más grandes puedan operar.</p><p><i>Erika Knierim, socia, Founders Law </i></p><h3>La falta de vivienda no es un problema desechable</h3><p>Cuando se le preguntó sobre una lista de posibles recortes en el presupuesto del próximo año, el columnista Rich Miller notó recientemente que la oficina del gobernador dijo que se habían recortado los fondos destinados a abordar la falta de vivienda debido a "una menor demanda".</p><p>Esta afirmación desafía la lógica en un momento en el que cientos de miles de habitantes de bajos ingresos de Illinois están siendo desestabilizados al perder el acceso a los beneficios del Programa de Asistencia Nutricional Suplementaria (SNAP), y el Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano (HUD) amenaza con desfinanciar muchas unidades de vivienda de apoyo permanente en todo el estado.</p><p>De hecho, el <a class="Link" href="https://www.dhs.state.il.us/OneNetLibrary/27897/documents/Homelessness/24-26_Home%20Illinois_Plan2%20(003)_A11Y.pdf" target="_blank" >Plan Home Illinois para prevenir y acabar con la falta de vivienda</a> ha identificado una escasez de 4,236 camas en refugios, 10,428 unidades de vivienda temporal y 10,972 unidades de vivienda de apoyo permanente en Illinois.</p><p>Aunque el conteo puntual del estado (un conteo de una noche de personas que experimentan la falta de vivienda requerido por HUD) mostró una disminución del 44% de 2024 a 2025, el número puede explicarse completamente por la disminución de migrantes recién llegados a Chicago. Si se excluye a los recién llegados del conteo, <a class="Link" href="https://www.dhs.state.il.us/OneNetLibrary/27897/documents/Homelessness/FY25AnnualReport%20(002).pdf" target="_blank" >la falta de vivienda en Illinois aumentó de alrededor de 10,000 en 2023 a casi 15,000 en 2025.</a></p><p>La falta de vivienda es un problema serio y creciente en Illinois, y los fondos para abordarlo no deberían figurar en la lista de recortes. Más bien, se requieren aumentos presupuestarios para prevención, albergue, vivienda y otras necesidades.</p><p>Hay propuestas sobre la mesa en Springfield para cobrar impuestos a los ricos y a las corporaciones con el fin de generar nuevos ingresos para el estado. No necesitamos recortar servicios a los residentes más vulnerables de nuestro estado. Hacemos un llamado a la Legislatura para que apruebe los proyectos de ley de ingresos progresivos y aumente, en lugar de disminuir, los fondos destinados a acabar con la falta de vivienda.</p><p><i>Julie Dworkin, co-directora ejecutiva, Instituto para el Bien Público </i></p><p><i>Bob Palmer, director de políticas, Housing Action Illinois </i></p><p><i>Doug Schenkelberg, director ejecutivo, Coalición de Chicago para Acabar con la Falta de Vivienda </i></p><h3>Uso ineficaz de los recursos de la Policía de Chicago</h3><p>¿Redadas a los vendedores ambulantes en el Loop o detenciones de <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/05/27/mayor-brandon-johnson-teen-takeovers-hyde-park-near-west-side-memorial-day-weekend-curfew-parent-responsibility-laws" target="_blank" >tomas de control de adolescentes</a>?</p><p>Comparemos la seguridad negativa de los oficiales y el público y los efectos financieros de las tomas de control de calles por adolescentes vs. los vendedores ambulantes en el centro.</p><p>¿Es el mismo funcionario de la Policía de Chicago que ideó la nueva política <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/cpd-pet-directive-limits-stray-and-abandoned-animal-drop-offs/" target="_blank" >que limita las opciones</a> para que los residentes lleven animales abandonados a las estaciones de policía, el mismo que decidió que deshacerse de los vendedores ambulantes en el Loop —como <a class="Link" href="https://www.cbsnews.com/chicago/news/street-vendors-chicago-loop-chicago-police/" target="_blank" >fue reportado la semana pasada</a> por CBS News Chicago— es un buen uso de los recursos policiales?.</p><p><i>Charles Carlson, Belmont-Cragin </i></p><h3>Control de multitudes</h3><p>Algunas personas están muy alteradas por estas tomas de control de los adolescentes. La gente está aquí simplemente divirtiéndose, como lo hicieron las masas el 6 de enero de 2021.</p><p><i>William Brown, Little Italy </i></p><h3>La presidenta interina de la CTA no es diferente a los líderes anteriores</h3><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2025/07/30/interim-cta-president-nora-leerhsen-permanent-post-dorval-carter" target="_blank" >Nora Leerhsen</a> debería ya ser nombrada presidenta permanente de la Autoridad de Tránsito de Chicago (CTA). Ha actuado el tiempo suficiente. Está haciendo un buen trabajo dejando que sus ineficientes castiguen a los trabajadores de la CTA por enfermarse y por reportar peligros mortales. ¡Démosle un Oscar también!</p><p><i>Eric Basir, delegado del sindicato Local 308 y electo de la Junta Ejecutiva de Mantenimiento de Vehículos del Local 308. </i></p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (AI) y editado por </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a></p>

entries.title: NASCAR Chicago Street Race could return in 2027: reports
entries.summary: <p>NASCAR is nearing a deal with the city to bring the Chicago Street Race back to Grant Park in 2027, according to media reports. </p><p>Block Club Chicago was the first to report that NASCAR was finalizing plans to hold the race again. The street race was held for three summers — 2023 through 2025 — over the July 4th weekend in Grant Park.</p><p>For the next time around, race organizers are looking to move the event up from July, holding it instead closer to the 2027 Sueños Festival (May 29-30) and Memorial Day (May 31), according to Block Club. </p><p>But no deal has formally been announced by the city or NASCAR. Jake DiGregorio, a spokesperson with NASCAR, told the Sun-Times "the 2027 schedule is still in development."</p><p>Leslie Recht, president of the Grant Park Advisory Council, shared the potential plan with Block Club and the Chicago Tribune. When reached by the Sun-Times, she declined to comment.</p><p>The Athletic, a sports outlet owned by The New York Times, first reported NASCAR's potential return nearly three weeks ago. </p><p>Ald. Brian Hopkins (2nd) told the Sun-Times he's aware the city is working on a deal, but he has not received a finalized agreement. Hopkins and his fellow downtown City Council members expect to be briefed on any new deal, he said. </p><p>In 2022, then-Mayor Lori Lightfoot inked a three-year contract with NASCAR to host the Chicago Street Race in Grant Park. That contract did allow for two possible one-year extensions in 2026 and 2027. </p><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson's office and a Chicago Parks District spokesperson did not immediately respond to requests for comment. </p><p><i>Contributing: David Struett</i> </p>

entries.title: Mayor's new human relations chair hopes to build bridges to Jewish community
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson’s choice of a "lifer" to lead Chicago’s Commission on Human Relations vowed Tuesday to repair the mayor’s frayed relationship with mainstream Jewish leaders.</p><p>Kenneth Gunn, a civil rights attorney who has spent more than three decades with the Commission on Human Relations, replaces Nancy Andrade, who resigned in March to protest what critics contend was an attempt by Johnson’s administration to whitewash a long-awaited report that was supposed to focus solely on antisemitism.</p><p>Gunn said he has “good friends” in the Jewish community who “know me and know what I stand for” because he’s worked with many of them for years.</p><p>The mayor’s relationship with leaders of the mainstream Jewish community has been frayed ever since Johnson cast the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2024/1/31/24057161/mayor-brandon-johnson-gaza-ceasefire-resolution-raucous-debate-clears-chambers" target="_blank" >tie-breaking vote</a> in favor of a nonbinding resolution demanding a ceasefire in the Israel-Hamas conflict.</p><p>But Gunn said he's determined to ease that tension with Johnson's support.</p><p>“Everything I’ve heard from the mayor is super-positive. He really, really wants to engage the Jewish community. And he wants me to make sure that we’re doing all we can ... to address anti-Jewish hate,” Gunn said.</p><p></p><p>Last week, Johnson unveiled a strategy to combat all manner of hate crimes that Jewish leaders condemned as an insensitive and inadequate response to the surge in anti-Jewish hate crimes.</p><p>Johnson’s plan called for creating a “Jewish Engagement Council to serve as a direct bridge for dialogue” between residents, community leaders and the mayor’s office, and an “Interconnected Chicago Council” to address “fragmentation between communities.”</p><p>The commission-approved report — triggered by a 58% rise in reported anti-Jewish hate crimes from 2023 to 2024 — recommended a dedicated task force to combat anti-Jewish hate, mandatory training on antisemitism for city employees, teachers and students in Chicago Public Schools and a dedicated unit within the Chicago Police Department to combat hate crimes.</p><p>Gunn said he favors the mayor’s version of the report because "hate fluctuates in terms of the targets.</p><p>"We’ve seen it against the LGBT community. During COVID, we saw the Asian community attacked. During the Gulf War and after 9/11, the Muslim-Arab community were most often victimized,” Gunn said.</p><p>“It does make sense to have a group of leaders in these communities working together to address hate because hate affects all of us."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-floatRight> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" There’s a lot of work to be done. I hope that Ken is the right guy to do it. I hope he can be,” said Goldwin, who serves as chief public affairs officer for the Jewish United Fund.</p><p>Rebecca Weininger, senior regional director for the Anti-Defamation League Midwest, has accused Johnson of “cherry-picking Jewish voices that are acceptable to him — either because they are anti-Zionist or because they are willing to go along with any crumbs that he is willing to feed them.”</p><p>But given what she called Gunn’s “nuanced understanding of the way that anti-Semitism shows up in Chicago,” Weininger said she is hopeful that the new commissioner will "stay true to the work that the commission has already done."</p><p>“I want him to take the sophisticated understanding that he is inheriting from the commission and use his influence for good on the council to ensure that this is not something that is vacuous, but has substance," she said.</p><p>Johnson’s relationship with mainstream Jewish leaders was further strained by the mayor’s refusal to fire his chief lobbyist, Kennedy Bartley, and remove Ald. Rossana Rodriguez Sanchez (33rd) as chair of the City Council’s Committee on Health and Human Relations for their social media posts viewed by Jewish leaders as antisemitic.</p><p>The mayor initially defended his appointment of the Rev. Mitchell Johnson as president of the Chicago Board of Education, only to have Johnson resign the following day after antisemitic comments were found on his social media pages.</p><p>Johnson also refused to remove artwork on display at the Cultural Center that a City Council majority viewed as antisemitic. </p><p>Gunn's goal is to ease the strain going forward.</p><p>“If people come together with open minds, we can do that,” he said.<br></p>

entries.title: Cubs’ rotation getting healthier with imminent Edward Cabrera, Matthew Boyd returns, but is it deep enough?
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ banged-up starting rotation is getting healthier.</p><p>Right-hander Edward Cabrera, the team’s big offseason pitching acquisition, and lefty Matthew Boyd, a 2025 All-Star and the team’s Opening Day starter, are both due back from injury soon.</p><p>Manager Craig Counsell said Tuesday that Cabrera, on the IL with a blister, will return during the upcoming weekend series with the Giants.</p><p>Boyd, meanwhile, made a rehab start with Triple-A Iowa on Sunday and will make another Saturday. Assuming all goes well, he’ll be, as Counsell put it, “good to go.”</p><p>The imminent returns are big deals for the Cubs, who saw their starting staff decimated by injuries in the first two months of the season. Righty Cade Horton was lost for the season to Tommy John surgery, while Boyd has been on the shelf for a month recovering from knee surgery.</p><p>“We need healthy bodies back,” Counsell said.</p><p>But Tuesday’s other pitching news showed the Cubs aren’t exactly out of the woods when it comes to dealing with future losses in the rotation.</p><p>The team sent Jordan Wicks back to Iowa after a pair of brief, ugly outings as a fill-in. Wicks was scorched for eight runs last week in Pittsburgh and got a quick hook after facing just 10 batters — and giving up another three runs — Sunday in St. Louis.</p><p>He returned to the minors with a gargantuan 15.63 ERA after just 6 1/3 innings of work, showing the mixed results the Cubs have seen as they’ve utilized their starting-pitching depth.</p><p>Though Wicks’ cameo wasn’t pretty, Ben Brown has shone. With a 1.92 ERA, Brown has been the team’s best pitcher this season.</p><p>But Javier Assad was shipped down to Iowa, too. Top prospect Jaxon Wiggins is working back from elbow inflammation. And Colin Rea hasn’t been quite as productive in a surprise rotation role as he was last season, his ERA at 4.70 after he finished last year with a career-best 3.95 mark in 32 games, all but five of which were starts.</p><p>“Most of the guys on the starting staff have gone through injuries, so when your teammate goes through it, you do your best to try to pick him up and help him,” Rea told the Sun-Times on Tuesday.</p><p>“I feel like I’ve been doing this, even when I was in Milwaukee. So I guess I’m somewhat used to it. … Whatever happens, I’m ready for it.”</p><p>Rea might need to stay on his toes. To make room for the returns of Cabrera and Boyd, the Cubs have already jettisoned Wicks, but Rea could be the odd man out, heading back to the bullpen to wait for the next injury absence, however lengthy.</p><p>“I don’t know what that’s going to look like. I haven’t thought about it too much,” Rea said. “If that does happen, it speaks to the position that we’re in. If we’re making moves like that, it shows our rotation is strong. But I guess we’ll cross that bridge when it comes.”</p><p>With the way some of the team’s other starters are performing, how long before they need to go searching for more options?</p><p>The Cubs have invested too much in Jameson Taillon and Shota Imanaga, two accomplished and respected veterans, to just toss them aside. But they have been shaky. Taillon has allowed more home runs than any pitcher in the majors, coming into his Tuesday night outing with 19 long balls on his tab. Imanaga isn’t far behind, with 13 long balls surrendered, and they allowed 10 homers apiece last month.</p><p>At 5.33, Cubs starters had the third-highest ERA in baseball in May.</p><p>As is the case for nearly every team nearly every year, pitching can be assumed to be a trade-deadline priority for Jed Hoyer’s front office. With growing expectations, Hoyer has shown a willingness to make moves for high-impact players, and he dealt highly regarded prospects away for Kyle Tucker and Cabrera in back-to-back offseasons.</p><p>But last summer, when adding a starting pitcher seemed almost mandatory, Hoyer didn’t pull the trigger on a deal. And the Cubs saw their starting pitchers run out of gas in the NLDS against the Brewers.</p><p>Can they prevent that problem from bringing another season to an earlier-than-desired end?</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: Sky injury report: No firm timeline for DiJonai Carrington, Azura Stevens still finding her legs
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON — The timeline for All-Defensive wing <b>DiJonai Carrington’s</b> return remains a mystery.</p><p>Carrington continues to rehab from ankle surgery in October and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky/2026/05/03/sky-defense-needs-dijonai-carrington-back-and-soon" target="_blank" >said on media day</a> that she didn’t want to publicize a specific timeline. Since then, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> haven’t given so much as an inkling about when she might return to practice — whether it’s before or after the All-Star break in July or somewhere in between.</p><p>But coach <b>Tyler Marsh</b> pushed back on <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/06/02/chicago-sky-risks-roster-construction/" target="_blank" >one report</a> that said the Sky signed Carrington knowing she might not play until after the FIBA World Cup break, which runs from Aug. 31 to Sept. 16. That would leave just eight days in the regular season.</p><p>‘‘We shouldn’t believe everything that we see and read,’’ Marsh said. ‘‘We are committed to the timeline that has been established. She’s progressing well, into on-court activities. ... We’re looking forward to getting her back.’’</p><p>Carrington seemed to back up Marsh. She reposted a tweet citing the report with a ‘‘cap’’ emoji — slang for ‘‘false.’’</p><p>In the meantime, the Sky are down to eight fully healthy players on their roster.</p><p>Their defense has held up through the injuries — it still ranks sixth in the league overall — but it has shown signs of sputtering, especially with rookie wing <b>Gabriela Jaquez</b> out with a knee injury.</p><p>They could use an infusion of the intelligence and athleticism Carrington brings on that end. Fans, however, will have to keep guessing about when that infusion will come.</p><p>For now, the primary glimpses come during the portion of practices open to the media, where Carrington typically is rehabbing and doing individual workouts.</p><p>She sprained her ankle in the playoffs last season and, after offseason surgery and rehab, had a follow-up procedure in mid-April to remove hardware from the joint.</p><h3>Running on limited minutes</h3><p>Forward <b>Azura Stevens</b> is another player the Sky would like to have at full throttle. She’s still on a minutes restriction — around 16 — and feels as though she’s still getting her legs under her after missing the first five games of the season with a bone bruise in her knee.</p><p>‘‘My body’s just getting used to the load that I’m taking on,’’ she said at the Sky’s shootaround Tuesday.</p><p>Stevens said there’s no exact science to determine her minutes; they depend on how she feels on the day of the game. If she’s feeling better, the medical team might bump them up; if not, they stay the same.</p><p>She acknowledged the challenge of finding her rhythm in spurts.</p><p>‘‘It’s really, really hard,’’ she said. ‘‘Just trying to get a flow because right when I feel like I’m getting going, I have to come out. But I understand it’s just the process right now.’’</p><h3>UCLA reunion</h3><p>Though Jaquez missed her third consecutive game, she at least got to have dinner with two former UCLA teammates in Mystics rookies <b>Lauren Betts</b> and <b>Angela Dugalic</b>.</p><p>Both lit up at the chance to talk about Jaquez.</p><p>‘‘Gabs is one of those players I hope I play with again someday,’’ Dugalic told the Sun-Times. ‘‘She’s so versatile. She does the little things, which end up being the big things.</p><p>‘‘She can do anything, from scoring in different ways to defending different people. She will be so tired, gasping for air, and still somehow finds a way to be the first one down the court.’’</p><p>Betts said she just misses seeing Jaquez’s face every day.</p><p>‘‘But thank God we all have phones, so we text and FaceTime all the time,’’ Betts said.</p><p></p><bsp-list-loadmore class="PageListH" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: Sean Burke: 'Thank God I get to play for the Chicago White Sox'
entries.summary: <p>MINNEAPOLIS — Sean Burke was feeling good after the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a>’ comeback victory Sunday at Rate Field against the Tigers. Though he was dealing with a lingering cold, his mental state overcame it.</p><p>“I should pitch sick more often,” he joked after throwing 5⅓ strong innings.</p><p>It was that state of mind that led Burke to share what he said later:</p><p>"I wake up every day, ‘Thank God I get to play for the Chicago White Sox.’ ”</p><p>On social media, where snarky comments are encouraged, that quote, unattributed, surely would’ve been followed by, “Said no one ever.”</p><p>But a burgeoning Sox starter said it, unprompted. He said it with a smile, giving a hint of being lighthearted, as when he suggested he should pitch sick. Still, he said it. On the record. For all to hear.</p><p>What made him say that?</p><p>“I meant that, but I kinda said it originally half-joking,” Burke told the Sun-Times on Monday. “I just have a really great appreciation for this group and the way we’re playing, the way everybody has bought into what we’re doing. Everybody’s playing hard; everybody’s playing the right way.”</p><p>Call it corny, but there is something special about this group. Its majority is young players who don’t know what they don’t know. But it also has a segment of veterans, and they sense a unique quality about the team’s togetherness.</p><p>“Grich told me day one, he’s like, ‘Man, this team’s something else,’ ” Burke said of Randal Grichuk, a 13-year vet who joined the Sox on May 4.</p><p>So what did Grichuk notice?</p><p>“It’s young, it’s energetic, it’s immature — not in a negative way,” Grichuk told the Sun-Times. “I actually talked to a couple guys [Sunday], because I wasn’t starting, on the bench, and they were both like, ‘I am genuinely excited and happy to wake up and come here and work.’ It’s good friends, it’s good vibes.”</p><p>Grichuk is playing for his eighth major-league team and sixth in four seasons. He played in 16 games for the Yankees this season before being released May 1. He’s as qualified as anyone to talk about clubhouse camaraderie, and he called the Sox’ situation “rare.”</p><p>“There’s definitely less cliques, more overall bonding here,” Grichuk said. “Most teams you have the bullpen, the starters, the young guys, the old guys all in their little cliques. But here, [the older guys] fit in well, and it’s great. It’s hard to put into words because I’ve not seen much like it, honestly.”</p><p>Burke appreciates those veterans, including Grichuk, Andrew Benintendi and Seranthony Dominguez, for accepting and accommodating the younger players.</p><p>“They understand it’s a younger team, and they enjoy how we’re playing,” Burke said. “There’s no walking on eggshells or anything like that. Younger guys coming in, they’re a little bit intimidated by an older clubhouse. But everybody from the top down has been doing a pretty good job of making everybody play free and relaxed.”</p><p>“I want to feel like they look at me as one of the boys,” Grichuk said, “not as I looked at some of the vets when I came up. You didn’t talk to them, you didn’t bother them.</p><p>“I’m not naming names, but one guy was giving me some jabs the other day, and a few other guys were like, ‘Uh oh.’ I laughed it off, and I said I’ll pay that back later. It’s fun, and it’s light. I’ve really enjoyed my time here so far.”</p><p>Burke’s “Thank God” quote drew a big smile from Sox general manager Chris Getz, who said he has heard and seen that sentiment in the clubhouse himself.</p><p>“It’s gratitude. It’s organic,” Getz told the Sun-Times. “He’s excited to come to work.”</p><p>By the sound of it, he isn’t the only one.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" entries.title: MLB marks Lou Gehrig Day, but Jon 'Boog' Sciambi has become an advocate for those with ALS
entries.summary: <p>For at least one night in Wrigley Field on Tuesday, these three initials were at least as important as PCA.</p><p>ALS.</p><p>Boog Sciambi is driven by a desire to see the day when all of us understand the implication of those letters for the ones stricken with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis. ALS is a progressive nervous system disease that affects how nerve cells communicate with your muscles. ALS leads to muscle weakness that gets worse over time, according to the Cleveland Clinic, and affects how you move, speak and breathe. It is a beast that shows no mercy.</p><p>Sciambi, the Cubs’ TV play-by-play man, wants us to remember ALS not just once a year on Lou Gehrig Day, as the Cubs observed Tuesday with pregame ceremonies honoring the memory of the New York Yankees’ Hall of Famer, along with fans with ALS and their families invited onto the field. On June 2, 1941, Gehrig succumbed to the affliction, which in the public mind quickly became known as Lou Gehrig's disease. </p><p>That’s a good start by MLB, which only a few years ago conceived Lou Gehrig Day. ALS should be regarded as baseball’s disease. But until a cure is found, there is work to be done, raising the millions necessary to do the research to find the cure. But just as important — and Boog might argue even more so — is sending an urgent message to those who are battling this rare affliction that they are not alone.</p><p>“When people are being affected by ALS,” Sciambi said, “their mobility starts to disintegrate and their ability to communicate declines, and so their world gets really small. So [it matters] when you’re able to reach out and say, ‘Hey, what’s up? Do you need help? Would you like to go to the Cubs game on Lou Gehrig Day? What can we do?’</p><p>“I just think I realized how small your world gets after a while when you’ve had the disease — that you just want to feel seen. And I didn’t realize that you have the ability to give that to people, to say, ‘Hey, we didn’t forget about you. What can we do to make today special for you?’ ”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/3bDuhFpQCRQ?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="LOU GEHRIG: Honoring a legend & fighting ALS | Cubs Live! (Lou Gehrig Day ⚾)"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>There is a cruel irony to ALS. Gehrig, its most famous victim, was known as the “Iron Horse” for his durability. He played in 2,130 consecutive games, a streak that ALS brought to an abrupt end on April 30, 1939. It wasn’t until seven weeks later, on Gehrig’s 36th birthday, that he announced his diagnosis.</p><p>His streak stood as the major-league record until another Hall of Famer, Cal Ripken Jr., broke it on Sept. 6, 1995, 56 years later. Gehrig died less than two years after he broke the news of his diagnosis.</p><p>And even a crueler irony: We are no closer to a cure than when Gehrig succumbed 85 years ago. To date, no one has survived ALS, the exact cause of which remains unknown. In about 10% of cases, ALS is inherited from a parent, according to the Mayo Clinic.</p><p>Typically, patients live another three to five years after diagnosis, although the Cleveland Clinic reports that 10 to 20% of patients live at least 10 years.</p><p>Sciambi adopted ALS care as a personal mission when Tim Sheehy, a childhood friend who grew up on Roosevelt Island in New York, was stricken with the disease in 2005. In the time he had left — two years — Sheehy founded a charitable organization, Project Main Street. Sciambi became an early supporter and has continued in that role for nearly 20 years.</p><p>Among other things, Sciambi and Project Main Street have partnered with the Chicago-based Obvious Shirts to sell T-shirts that say “End ALS” in the colors of all 30 major-league teams. For the sixth consecutive year, the Cubs and Sciambi’s employer, Marquee Sports Network, are sponsoring an on-line auction to benefit Project Main Street (you can bid at <a class="Link" href="https://www.cubs.com/alsauction" target="_blank" >cubs.com/alsauction</a>.) In addition, the charitable arm of MLB is also conducting an auction in which one of the items is a Pete Crow-Armstrong-autographed bat.</p><p>“I mean, look, you’re trying to raise money, and you’re trying to help people with their quality of life, but there’s that intangible component where you can do this thing for people that I hadn’t really contemplated,’’ Sciambi said.</p><p>Making people feel seen. Making people feel like they haven’t been forgotten.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Today, we play for No. 4.<br><br>Today, we play for the cure. <a href="https://x.com/hashtag/LouGehrigDay?src=hash&ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">#LouGehrigDay</a> <a href="https://t.co/s3Sx88qnCx">pic.twitter.com/s3Sx88qnCx</a></p>— MLB (@MLB) <a href="https://x.com/MLB/status/2061901126245507493?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 2, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>“There’s an element of it that’s just so [expletive] sad, because ultimately everybody dies,” Sciambi said. “But there are families that I stay in touch with, and that’s really cool.”</p><p>Sciambi went to school at Boston College. That’s where the captain of the baseball team, Pete Frates, was diagnosed with ALS and, together with a New Yorker, Pat Quinn, who was diagnosed with the disease around the same time, came up with the Ice Bucket Challenge, which raised millions for research. Sciambi remains friends with John and Nancy Frates, Pete’s parents.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="113" height="200" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/QFXw4oHIajc?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Michael Jordan does the ALS Ice Bucket Challenge"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>Stephen Piscotty, who was an outfielder for the Athletics, lost his mom, Gretchen, to ALS. His dad, Mike Piscotty, has spearheaded numerous fundraising endeavors for ALS research. He is in regular contact with Boog.</p><p>The late Chris Snow, an elegant baseball and hockey writer who was hired by the NHL’s Flames for his groundbreaking work in data analysis for that sport, lost dad Bob, two uncles and a cousin to ALS before being diagnosed himself. Boog gave Snow’s family a lasting memory when he invited Chris and Kelsie Snow and their two children, Cohen and Willa, onto the field.</p><p>And, perhaps most poignantly, Sciambi became acquainted with MLB researcher extraordinaire Sarah Langs when they worked together for ESPN during the pandemic. Sciambi was broadcasting from ESPN’s studios in Bristol, Connecticut; Langs, who had once been sports editor of the University of Chicago Maroon, provided him with the kind of info only she can provide.</p><p>If there is a face of ALS in MLB today, it is the unwavering smile of Langs, who continues to work through all that ALS has thrown at her, all the while tweeting out, “Baseball is the Best!” on a daily basis, multiple times a day.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">😭😭😭😭 <br><br>Thanks sooo much to everyone involved 🫶 <a href="https://t.co/5q8M6yn6uM">https://t.co/5q8M6yn6uM</a></p>— Sarah Langs (@SlangsOnSports) <a href="https://x.com/SlangsOnSports/status/2061953462175216022?ref_src=twsrc%5Etfw">June 2, 2026</a></blockquote> <script async src="https://platform.x.com/widgets.js" charset="utf-8"></script> </div> </div> </div></div><p>When Sarah told her best friend, baseball reporter Mandy Bell, of her diagnosis, Mandy would later write, she cried.</p><p>“I’m sorry,’’ Sarah said.</p><p>“What on earth are you apologizing for?’’ Mandy responded.</p><p>“Because I don’t want to make you sad,’’ Sarah said.</p><p>We’re sorry, Sarah. Like Mandy Bell, we, too, are sad. But we are in awe of your courage, and of Boog’s compassion. And we, too, live in hope.<br></p>

entries.title: Trump administration is scrapping $1.8B fund meant to compensate president’s allies, Blanche says
entries.summary: <p>WASHINGTON — The Trump administration is scrapping plans to create a $1.8 billion fund meant to compensate allies of the Republican president, the Justice Department’s top official said Tuesday in retreating from a program that faced setbacks in the courts and a fierce political backlash that had threatened to stall key elements of the White House agenda.</p><p>“We are not moving forward with the fund, period,” Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche said in response to questions at a House hearing on the Justice Department budget.</p><p>"Not moving forward, ever?” asked Rep. Grace Meng, a New York Democrat.</p><p>“Correct,” Blanche answered.</p><p>The blunt declaration marked an extraordinary, and rare, turnabout for a Trump Justice Department that just two weeks ago had pronounced the fund as an appropriate measure to make up for what officials insist was weaponized law enforcement during President Joe Biden’s Democratic administration. The fund has since been paused by a judge and lambasted by both Democrats and Republicans alike who said they were troubled by a lack of oversight as well as the potential for payouts to participants in the violent Jan. 6, 2021 riot at the U.S. Capitol.</p><p>Republicans had demanded reassurances that plans for the fund were off the table before they would move forward with legislation funding President Donald Trump’s immigration enforcement agencies.</p><p>When word of the settlement broke, the Senate was already navigating tricky passage of the immigration legislation with an added $1 billion in White House security costs — including for Trump’s ballroom project.</p><p>Furious, Senate Republicans jettisoned the White House security money from the bill and made clear they would not pass the legislation at all unless the White House made major changes to the settlement.</p><p>The $1.776 billion “Anti-Weaponization Fund” was established to resolve Trump’s lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service over the leak of his tax returns. As part of that deal, the IRS agreed to drop all pending probes of Trump over whether he’s paid his fair share of taxes.</p><p>Pressed over whether it was also abandoning that part of the deal, Blanche said “nothing has changed with that,” and said the administration was abandoning only the plans to create the $1.8 billion fund.</p><p>The hearing Tuesday before a House Appropriations subcommittee was scheduled for discussion of the Justice Department’s budget, but lawmakers quickly focused their questioning on the fund.</p><p>"This administration has engaged in what are perhaps the most brazen acts of flagrant corruption I’ve ever seen,” said Rep. Rosa DeLauro, a Democrat from Connecticut. “And you are at the center of many of them, Mr. Blanche.”</p><p>Signs of the retreat surfaced Monday when a person familiar with the matter said the Republican president was now reconsidering whether to move forward with the fund established to resolve his lawsuit against the Internal Revenue Service over the leak of his tax returns. The Justice Department also said Monday it would comply with a Virginia court temporarily blocking the administration’s “Anti-Weaponization Fund,” effectively agreeing to pause the plan for at least two weeks.</p><p>Another judge in Florida raised the prospect of reopening the IRS lawsuit because of “grievous allegations” of improper dealing made against the administration by settlement critics.<br></p>

entries.title: Byrne Elementary community rallies behind paralyzed clerk facing job loss
entries.summary: <p>After a car crash with a drunken driver left her paralyzed, Byrne Elementary clerk Judy Mahoney overcame barriers to remain employed. Now, Chicago Public Schools may cut the position she fought to keep.</p><p>Mahoney, 54, faces termination June 30 — the official end of the school year — because CPS plans to eliminate the school clerk position at Byrne Elementary in Garfield Ridge.</p><p>She has worked for CPS for 23 years, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2021/5/25/22453306/byrne-elementary-judy-mahoney-clerk-wheelchair-accessible-school-job-funding" target="_blank" >previous eight years</a> at Byrne Elementary.</p><p>In 2017, a car crash with a drunken driver paralyzed her from the waist down.</p><p>Before her current job, Mahoney worked for more than two decades at Whittier Elementary in Pilsen, but she was forced to switch schools after becoming paralyzed because that school is not wheelchair accessible, she said.</p><p>Dozens of Mahoney’s supporters, including Byrne Elementary students and staff, and Chicago Teachers Union representatives, gathered outside the Garfield Ridge school Tuesday afternoon to demand she keep her job at Byrne.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div its entrances, Frank Lally, an education policy analyst with Access Living, said roughly 50% of CPS schools are fully ADA compliant.</p><p>Brooklyn Casper, a 6th grade student at Byrne Elementary, called Mahoney a “star” of their school. She said Mahoney immediately made her feel that she belonged at the school on her first day.</p><p>“If you have ever walked into our main office, you know it is a very busy place. Phones are ringing, people are walking in and out and there are always millions of things happening at once. But Ms. Mahoney handles the chaos like a pro,” Brooklyn said. “No matter how crowded it gets, she’s always right there helping teachers, students and parents with whatever they need. She always greets us with warm 'good mornings.'”</p><p>Students gathered Tuesday held signs, one reading, “No Mahoney, that’s baloney!” and another reading, "Accessibility is not optional.”</p><p>Other supporters said Mahoney is an essential employee to the school who helps direct people in the building, reassure parents, comfort students and assist teachers with paperwork and other needs.</p><p>“She is an example of professionalism,” said Robert Gebel, a 6th grade literature teacher. “And the words of encouragement that she offers these kids in a proud, confident voice, reassuring demeanor every day, the students see a lady — a woman in a wheelchair who is confident, a woman who is kind, a woman who is responsible, a woman who is resilient with dignity, and a woman who is successful. Can we even find a better example for our students?”</p>

entries.title: Bridge the seasons with a bowl of spring pea pasta
entries.summary: <p>This simple pasta dish is both fresh and comforting — it bridges the transition from the cool freshness of spring to the relaxed warmth of summer. Green sweet peas and delicate pea shoots weave through this simple bowl of orecchiette. It's bound together by a cream sauce infused with crispy pancetta. A splash of chicken stock adds depth of flavor to the sauce while balancing the richness of the cream.</p><p>You may be tempted to use fresh peas in this recipe, but defrosted frozen peas are preferable. They are guaranteed to remain bright and sweet, with minimal cooking required to heat them through, making them an ideal staple for easy weeknight cooking. (Save those fresh peas in their pods for healthy snacking.) Pea shoots are the delicate leaves, stems and tendrils of the snow pea plant. They are often packaged with other microgreens and fresh herbs. If you are unable to access them, they can be omitted. For a vegetarian option, omit the pancetta and substitute vegetable stock for the chicken stock.</p><h3>Spring Pea Pasta</h3><p>Active time: 30 minutes<br>Total time: 30 minutes<br>Yield: Serves 4 to 5</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p>1 pound orecchiette<br>1 tablespoon olive oil<br>4 ounces pancetta, finely diced<br>1 garlic clove, grated<br>1/4 teaspoon crushed red pepper flakes<br>1 cup heavy cream<br>1/3 cup chicken stock<br>1/2 teaspoon kosher salt<br>1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper<br>1 cup frozen peas, defrosted<br>1/2 cup (packed) finely grated pecorino Romano cheese<br>1 1/2 cups pea shoots, loosely packed<br>1 tablespoon finely chopped fresh mint leaves<br>1/2 teaspoon finely grated lemon zest</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Bring a large pot of salted water to a rolling boil. Add the pasta and cook until al dente according to the package instructions. Drain, reserving 1/2 cup of the cooking water.</p><p>While the pasta is cooking, heat the oil in a skillet over medium heat. Add the pancetta and saute until the fat renders and it begins to crisp, 3 to 4 minutes. Transfer the pancetta to a plate lined with a paper towel.</p><p>Drain all but 1 tablespoon fat from the skillet. Add the garlic and red pepper flakes and saute over medium heat until fragrant, about 30 seconds. Add the cream, stock, salt and black pepper. Bring to a simmer, then reduce the heat to low. Continue to simmer until the cream is slightly reduced and thickened, 4 to 5 minutes, stirring frequently.</p><p>Add the peas and pancetta and stir to heat through, about 1 minute. Add the pasta and cheese and stir to combine. If too thick, add the reserved pasta water, 1 tablespoon at a time, to your desired consistency.</p><p>Remove the pan from the heat and stir in the pea shoots, mint, and lemon zest. Serve warm.</p><p><i>Lynda Balslev is an award-winning writer, cookbook author and recipe developer, and authors the blog TasteFood.</i></p>
entries.author: Lynda Balslev | TasteFood

entries.title: Mayor Brandon Johnson’s Springfield wins put Chicago ‘in the mix’ for Bears stadium
entries.summary: <p>Springfield’s stalled drive for <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears-stadium" target="_blank" ><u>Bears stadium</u></a> legislation and lingering questions about the potential playing field in Hammond, Indiana, leave Chicago as the team’s best play for a new dome.</p><p>That’s according to Mayor Brandon Johnson, who had plenty of cause for end-zone celebrations after Illinois lawmakers advanced several of his top priorities at the end of their spring session and just as importantly <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/06/01/bears-stadium-arlington-heights-hammond-sprinfield-house-senate-bill-kevin-warren-george-mccaskey-nfl" target="_blank" ><u>spiked a bill</u></a> that would have cleared the Bears’ path out of Soldier Field to the suburbs.</p><p>“There's no plan in Hammond. There's none of that in the suburbs,” Johnson told WBEZ and the Sun-Times on Tuesday. “We are already further along than any other site that might even be considered.”</p><p>Johnson also can take some credit for clearing the path for a new digital advertising tax that made it into the state budget, along with a social media tax <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/03/13/chicago-social-media-tax-lawsuit-facebook-tiktok-block-brandon-johnson" target="_blank" ><u>mirroring the one his administration implemented</u></a> last year — evidence that he’s finally breaking the line of scrimmage in Springfield, he says.</p><p>“I've called for progressive revenue in Springfield from the very time in which I was sworn into this seat,” Johnson said. “We are now finally seeing the results of our hard labor and our advocacy.”</p><p>Chicago Democrats reluctant to lose the Bears didn’t need much convincing from the mayor to tank the megaproject bill the team has long sought, but the 11th-hour public stadium pitch approved by the Illinois Senate validated his 2024 pitch for a new dome south of Soldier Field, Johnson said.</p><p>“Not only did we have a publicly owned stadium that expanded green space, we were moving forward with conversations around the terms of an agreement,” Johnson said of his administration’s dealings with the team since he and Bears president Kevin Warren pushed for the lakefront.</p><p>“That's been ongoing, and the hope is that Springfield, after what they've done in this last session, that Springfield engages with the Bears, with the city and all stakeholders collectively, to come up with a… plan that shows the viability of what we've already put forward,” he said, unfazed by Warren’s stated timeline of announcing their destination by early summer.</p><p>The new bill sponsored by state Sen. Bill Cunningham, D-Chicago, would allow Chicago, Arlington Heights and other Cook County municipalities with populations of 70,000 or more to create stadium financing authorities and negotiate with teams. Johnson called it “a framework that places Chicago right in the mix to keep the Bears… and that's what we've always said that we needed.”</p><p>Johnson wasn’t the only official heartened by Springfield’s inaction. Indiana Gov. Mike Braun said Tuesday he expected it to result in a team announcement “in less than a month” that they’ll break ground in Hammond, where Hoosier lawmakers have authorized a slew of new taxes to help fund a stadium.</p><p>Indiana Gov. Mike Braun suggested it was a no-brainer for the Bears to move to "a place that runs like Indiana, triple-A credit rating, where you get a lot more stadium built for the money you're going to invest, where you've got friendly guidelines to have a business, in general, and where you're not going to be taxed out of existence.</p><p> “I think that is what they're actually looking at,” Braun said at an unrelated news conference in Indianapolis.</p><p> Johnson, meanwhile, argued “there’s no comparison. There's no traffic study in Arlington Heights. There's no environmental study in Hammond. There are no terms of agreement.”</p><p>As for other downstate wins, Johnson, with dozens of other Illinois mayors, was successful in fending off Pritzker’s proposed cut to the share of income taxes local municipalities receive, known as the Local Government Distributive Fund.</p><p>“I was able to lead a delegation from the most northern part of the state to the southern part of the state, a bipartisan approach to protect the local government distributed fund,” Johnson said.</p><p>Johnson has been heavily criticized for his Springfield agenda, which hasn’t yielded the types of new progressive revenue he campaigned on winning.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker recently joined the chorus, slamming Johnson for “show[ing] up in May” with “a bunch of demands”</p><p>“It's unfortunate that's happened most years,” Pritzker said. “This is kind of typical, the mayor has shown up every spring at the end of session.”</p><p>On Tuesday, Johnson rebuffed the insult.</p><p>“The last couple of sessions, quite frankly, it came down to what the final hours before the budget was actually passed. I mean, some could argue that I was there too early,” he said, chuckling.</p>
entries.author: Michael Puente | WBEZ
